unit.title: A Changing Nation Study Tool
unit.subtitle: Factories, cities, and twelve million new Americans. Learn the vocabulary, explore the era, and track your progress.
unit.essentialQuestion: How did industry, cities, and immigration remake America — and who built it?

vocabulary.definition: The shift from making goods by hand at home to making them by machine in factories
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Imagine everything you own being handmade, one at a time — then suddenly machines can crank out thousands of copies a day. That switch changed where people lived, what jobs looked like, and who got rich.
vocabulary.example: Industrialization turned steel-making from small forges into giant mills employing thousands of workers
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Industrialization is the shift from making goods by hand to making them by machine in factories. Between 1877 and 1915 it transformed America faster than any change before it. The factories made a few owners enormously rich, but they were run by millions of workers, many of them immigrants.

vocabulary.definition: The rail line completed in 1869 that connected the East Coast to the Pacific for the first time
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Before it, crossing America took months by wagon. After it, about a week by train. The famous photo shows the owners' golden spike — but the track itself was laid largely by Chinese and Irish immigrant workers whose faces mostly got left out of the picture.
vocabulary.example: The Transcontinental Railroad met at Promontory Summit, Utah, in 1869, built in large part by thousands of Chinese laborers
vocabulary.typingSnippet: The Transcontinental Railroad, completed in 1869, linked the East Coast to the Pacific by rail. It moved people, goods, and ideas across the country at a speed no one had imagined. The companies got the glory, but immigrant workers, including thousands of Chinese laborers, actually built the track.

vocabulary.definition: A business owned by many investors who share its profits and its risks
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Instead of one owner, a corporation is owned in slices by lots of people who buy shares. That structure let businesses raise huge amounts of money — enough to build railroads, steel mills, and oil empires.
vocabulary.example: Andrew Carnegie's steel business grew into a corporation worth hundreds of millions of dollars
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A corporation is a business owned by many investors who share its profits and risks. Selling shares let companies raise enormous sums of money, enough to build railroads and steel mills. The corporation made industrial giants possible, for better and for worse.

vocabulary.definition: A company that controls an entire industry, eliminating real competition
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: When one company owns the whole game — every competitor bought out or crushed — it can charge whatever it wants and pay workers whatever it wants. Rockefeller's Standard Oil controlled about ninety percent of America's oil.
vocabulary.example: Standard Oil became a monopoly by buying up or undercutting nearly every rival oil refiner
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A monopoly is a company that controls an entire industry and faces no real competition. Standard Oil controlled about ninety percent of American oil refining at its peak. Monopolies could set any price and any wage, which is why workers and reformers fought to break them up.

vocabulary.definition: A production method where each worker repeats one small task as the product moves past them
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Instead of one person building a whole product, the product slides down a line and each worker does one step, over and over, all day. Blazingly fast for the company — mind-numbing for the worker.
vocabulary.example: Assembly line methods eventually let Ford build a car in about ninety minutes instead of over twelve hours
vocabulary.typingSnippet: An assembly line moves a product past a line of workers, each repeating one small task. It made goods faster and cheaper than the world had ever seen. It also turned skilled craft work into repetitive labor, one reason workers began to organize.

vocabulary.definition: The rapid growth of cities as people move to them for work and opportunity
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Factories needed workers, so people flooded into cities — from American farms and from across the ocean. Chicago went from about 300,000 people to 1.7 million in just thirty years. Cities grew faster than anyone could plan for.
vocabulary.example: Urbanization pushed Chicago from around 300,000 people in 1870 to about 1.7 million by 1900
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Urbanization is the rapid growth of cities as people move to them for work. Industrial jobs pulled millions off farms and across oceans into American cities. The newcomers built the cities and powered the factories, but the cities were rarely ready for them.

vocabulary.definition: A crowded, low-cost apartment building where many urban workers and immigrant families lived
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Picture a whole family — sometimes two — in one or two dark rooms, in a building packed with dozens of families, sharing water and air shafts. Tenements were what the people who built the modern city could actually afford to live in.
vocabulary.example: Jacob Riis photographed New York tenements to show comfortable Americans how the other half lived
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A tenement was a crowded, low-cost apartment building where many workers and immigrant families lived. Rooms were dark, air was bad, and disease spread fast. Jacob Riis photographed tenement life to force comfortable Americans to see how the other half lived.

vocabulary.definition: A very tall steel-framed building that allowed crowded cities to grow upward instead of outward
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Cheap steel plus the elevator equals a brand-new idea: when a city runs out of ground, build into the sky. The skyline itself became a symbol of the new industrial America.
vocabulary.example: Chicago's Home Insurance Building, finished in 1885, is often called the first skyscraper
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A skyscraper is a very tall steel-framed building that lets a crowded city grow upward. Cheap steel and the safety elevator made them possible in the 1880s. Every skyline photo from the era is also a photo of the ironworkers who riveted it together, hundreds of feet up.

vocabulary.definition: An organization that traded favors, jobs, and services for votes in order to control city government
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: In chaotic, fast-growing cities, machine bosses offered immigrants real help — a job, coal in winter, a translator at court — and collected loyalty and votes in return. Helpful and corrupt at the same time, which is what makes them interesting.
vocabulary.example: New York's Tammany Hall political machine helped immigrants find jobs and housing, then counted on their votes
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A political machine traded favors, jobs, and services for votes to control city government. Machine bosses often gave immigrants real help that no one else offered. The price was corruption, as bosses skimmed money from the very city services their voters depended on.

vocabulary.definition: Moving to a new country to live there permanently
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Between 1880 and 1915, more than twenty million people left everything familiar and moved to the United States — chasing work, fleeing hunger or persecution, following family. They became the workforce that built modern America.
vocabulary.example: Immigration brought millions of Italians, Poles, Russian Jews, Chinese, and Japanese to American cities and railroads
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Immigration is moving to a new country to live there permanently. Between 1880 and 1915, more than twenty million immigrants came to the United States. They dug the subways, sewed the clothing, and worked the mills, which makes them a huge part of the answer to who built modern America.

vocabulary.definition: The immigration station in New York Harbor where millions of mostly European immigrants entered the United States
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: For over twelve million people, America began here: a huge inspection hall where doctors checked your health, officials checked your papers, and a few nerve-wracking hours decided your future. Most made it through in a day.
vocabulary.example: An Italian family arriving at Ellis Island in 1905 might pass through inspection in a few hours and sleep in Manhattan that night
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Ellis Island was the immigration station in New York Harbor where millions of mostly European immigrants entered the United States. It opened in 1892 and processed over twelve million people. For many families, the story of becoming American starts in its great inspection hall.

vocabulary.definition: The immigration station in San Francisco Bay where immigrants, mostly from Asia, were processed and often detained for long periods
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The West Coast's version of Ellis Island — but with a harder story. Because of anti-Chinese laws, arrivals from Asia faced interrogations and detentions that could last weeks or months. Detainees carved poems about the wait into the barracks walls; you can still read them.
vocabulary.example: A Chinese teenager at Angel Island might be questioned for weeks about tiny details of his home village to prove his identity
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Angel Island was the immigration station in San Francisco Bay, opened in 1910, where immigrants mostly from Asia were processed. Unlike Ellis Island, arrivals often faced weeks or months of interrogation and detention under anti-Chinese laws. Poems carved into the barracks walls still record how it felt to wait.

vocabulary.definition: The belief that native-born Americans should be favored over immigrants, and that immigration should be restricted
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: The push-back against newcomers: fear that immigrants would take jobs, change the culture, or vote the wrong way. Nativism produced real laws with real consequences — the Chinese Exclusion Act banned an entire nationality for decades.
vocabulary.example: Nativism drove the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, the first federal law to ban immigration by nationality
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Nativism is the belief that native-born Americans deserve favor over immigrants. In this era it fueled discrimination and laws like the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882. The tension is striking: the nation depended on immigrant labor while many Americans campaigned to shut immigrants out.

vocabulary.definition: The spread of foods, words, music, beliefs, and customs from one culture into another
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Cultures don't stay in separate boxes — they mix. Pizza, bagels, chow mein, new words, new music, new holidays: every immigrant community changed America while it was becoming American. It's how the answer to 'what's American?' keeps growing.
vocabulary.example: Cultural diffusion is why an American school lunch can include pizza, teriyaki, and tacos without anyone finding it strange
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Cultural diffusion is the spread of foods, words, music, and customs from one culture into another. Every immigrant community changed American culture even as it adapted to it. Modern American food, language, and music are the running record of that exchange.

vocabulary.definition: An organization of workers who band together to demand better pay, hours, and working conditions
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: One worker asking for a raise can be fired and replaced. Ten thousand workers asking together are much harder to ignore. Unions were workers' answer to the enormous power of the corporations they worked for.
vocabulary.example: The American Federation of Labor united skilled workers to bargain for higher wages and an eight-hour day
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A labor union is an organization of workers who band together to demand better pay and conditions. Alone, a worker could be fired and replaced in an hour; together, workers had real power. Unions argued that the people who built the nation's wealth deserved a fair share of it.

vocabulary.definition: A protest in which workers refuse to work until their demands are met
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: A union's most powerful weapon: everyone stops working at once, and the factory, railroad, or mine goes silent. Strikes were risky — strikers could lose their jobs or worse — but they forced the country to pay attention.
vocabulary.example: During the Pullman Strike of 1894, railroad workers across the country stopped trains to protest wage cuts
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A strike is a protest in which workers refuse to work until their demands are met. When thousands struck at once, factories and railroads simply stopped. Strikes like Pullman in 1894 were risky and sometimes turned violent, but they made workers impossible to ignore.

vocabulary.definition: A factory or workshop with long hours, low pay, and unsafe conditions
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Twelve-hour days, six days a week, in a cramped room with locked doors and no safety rules — often sewing the clothes comfortable Americans wore. The Triangle Shirtwaist Fire showed the whole country what those locked doors cost.
vocabulary.example: The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory was a sweatshop where 146 workers, mostly young immigrant women, died in a 1911 fire
vocabulary.typingSnippet: A sweatshop is a factory with long hours, low pay, and unsafe conditions. Many were garment shops staffed by young immigrant women working twelve-hour days. The Triangle Shirtwaist Fire of 1911 killed 146 of these workers and finally forced new safety laws.

vocabulary.definition: The use of children as workers in factories, mines, and mills
vocabulary.simpleExplanation: Kids your age and younger worked full shifts — sorting coal, running spinning machines, selling newspapers at dawn — because their families needed the pay. Lewis Hine's photographs of these kids helped convince America to change the law.
vocabulary.example: Lewis Hine photographed eight-year-old coal breakers and mill girls to expose child labor to the public
vocabulary.typingSnippet: Child labor is the use of children as workers in factories, mines, and mills. In 1900, well over a million American children worked full shifts instead of attending school. Lewis Hine's photographs of these children became some of the most persuasive evidence reformers ever had.

timelineEvents.title: Transcontinental Railroad Completed
timelineEvents.description: East and West coasts are linked by rail at Promontory Summit, built largely by Chinese and Irish immigrant workers

timelineEvents.title: Telephone Patented
timelineEvents.description: Alexander Graham Bell patents the telephone, beginning a communication revolution

timelineEvents.title: Edison's Practical Light Bulb
timelineEvents.description: Thomas Edison's lab produces a workable electric light, and cities soon glow after dark

timelineEvents.title: Chinese Exclusion Act
timelineEvents.description: Nativism becomes federal law: the first act to ban immigration by nationality

timelineEvents.title: Haymarket Affair
timelineEvents.description: A Chicago labor rally for the eight-hour day ends in a deadly bombing, and unions face a fierce backlash

timelineEvents.title: Hull House Founded
timelineEvents.description: Jane Addams opens a Chicago settlement house offering classes, child care, and help to immigrant neighbors

timelineEvents.title: Ellis Island Opens
timelineEvents.description: The New York Harbor station begins processing what will become over twelve million immigrants

timelineEvents.title: Pullman Strike
timelineEvents.description: A strike against wage cuts spreads across the nation's railroads until federal troops break it

timelineEvents.title: Angel Island Station Opens
timelineEvents.description: The San Francisco Bay station begins processing and often detaining immigrants, mostly from Asia

timelineEvents.title: Triangle Shirtwaist Fire
timelineEvents.description: A fire kills 146 garment workers, mostly young immigrant women, and spurs new workplace safety laws

reflectionPrompts: How does {term} help answer the question of who really built modern America?
How would an immigrant worker, a factory owner, and a city kid each describe {term} differently?
Where do you see something like {term} still shaping cities, work, or immigration today?
